Lecture 8

Matrix Lie groups and their Lie algebras

What this lecture does

Part II begins. We define matrix Lie groups — closed subgroups of GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C) — and develop the matrix exponential, using it to attach to every matrix Lie group its Lie algebra; we compute these algebras for the classical groups, prove they are closed under the commutator, and establish in what sense the exponential bridges the two structures: a perfect dictionary locally, a subtler one globally. Complexification and the physicist’s Hermitian generators close the lecture.

Problems · 6 Notes (PDF) Sheet (PDF)

Matrix space, and the definition of a matrix Lie group

Part I studied symmetry in finite supply: groups whose elements can be listed, summed over, averaged. The groups of Part II — rotations through every angle, boosts to every velocity, phases of every argument — form continua, and the single new capability this brings is the one this lecture is built around: differentiation. Differentiating a continuous group at its identity produces a linear object, the Lie algebra, on which nearly every computation of Part II will be performed; the matrix exponential climbs back up. This lecture constructs both ends of the bridge and crosses it in both directions.

Notation. The operator a representation assigns to a group element, written ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) in Part I, is written Π(g)\Pi(g)Π(g) from here on (where it usually carries a continuous label); the two symbols denote the same object, and the function action (Π(g)ψ)(x)=ψ(g−1x)(\Pi(g)\psi)(x)=\psi(g^{-1}x)(Π(g)ψ)(x)=ψ(g−1x) of Lecture 3 is unchanged.

Everything happens inside the space Mn(C)M_n(\C)Mn​(C) of complex n×nn\times nn×n matrices, the vector space Cn2\C^{n^2}Cn2 in a matrix costume, measured with the operator norm ∥X∥=sup⁡v≠0∣Xv∣/∣v∣\norm{X}=\sup_{v\neq 0}\abs{Xv}/\abs{v}∥X∥=supv=0​∣Xv∣/∣v∣. The norm obeys the triangle inequality and, crucially, is submultiplicative, ∥XY∥≤∥X∥∥Y∥\norm{XY}\le\norm{X}\norm{Y}∥XY∥≤∥X∥∥Y∥; every eigenvalue of XXX obeys ∣λ∣≤∥X∥\abs{\lambda}\le\norm{X}∣λ∣≤∥X∥. All norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent (analysis), so convergence in ∥⋅∥\norm{\cdot}∥⋅∥ is entrywise convergence, Mn(C)M_n(\C)Mn​(C) is complete, and compact means closed and bounded (Heine–Borel). The algebra respects the topology: multiplication and det⁡\detdet are polynomial in the entries, hence continuous, so GL(n,C)=det⁡−1(C∖{0})\GL(n,\C)=\det\nolimits^{-1}\bigl(\C\setminus\{0\}\bigr)GL(n,C)=det−1(C∖{0}) is an open subset of Mn(C)M_n(\C)Mn​(C), on which inversion is continuous (Cramer’s formula). No topology beyond such metric-space language will be needed.

Definition 8.1 (Matrix Lie group). A matrix Lie group is a subgroup GGG of GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C) that is closed as a subset of GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C): whenever Am∈GA_m\in GAm​∈G converge to a matrix AAA with det⁡A≠0\det A\neq 0detA=0, the limit AAA lies in GGG.

Closedness is relative to GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C), not Mn(C)M_n(\C)Mn​(C): sequences in GGG may converge to singular matrices, about which the definition is silent. Thus GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C) itself qualifies, although diag⁡(1/m,1,…,1)\operatorname{diag}(1/m,1,\dots,1)diag(1/m,1,…,1) escapes it in the limit; and since entrywise reality is a closed condition, GL(n,R)\GL(n,\R)GL(n,R) qualifies too. Why insist on closedness? Because subgroups of GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C) can be strange in a way no symmetry group of physics is.

Example 8.2 (A line wound densely on a torus). Fix α\alphaα irrational and let Gα={(eit00eiαt):t∈R}⊂GL(2,C),G_\alpha=\left\{ \begin{pmatrix} e^{\ii t} & 0\\ 0 & e^{\ii\alpha t}\end{pmatrix} : t\in\R\right\}\subset\GL(2,\C),Gα​={(eit0​0eiαt​):t∈R}⊂GL(2,C), a respectable subgroup: the line R\RR wound with slope α\alphaα around the torus U(1)×U(1)\U(1)\times\U(1)U(1)×U(1) of diagonal unitaries. The winding never closes up, and the closure of GαG_\alphaGα​ is the whole torus (Sheet 8): a one-parameter family whose limits fill a two-parameter family. Closedness excludes exactly this pathology — and it legitimises the limit arguments from which every theorem of this lecture springs.

Remark 8.3 (Prerequisites, quoted freely). Part II draws on the prerequisites at full strength: from analysis, the Heine–Borel theorem and (once, in Theorem 8.31) the inverse function theorem; from linear algebra, the Schur triangularisation and the spectral normal forms of unitary and of special orthogonal matrices. Each use is flagged; everything else is proved.

The zoo: closedness, compactness, connectedness

The matrix groups of Lecture 1 return as protagonists, and one pattern verifies them all: each is carved out of GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C) by equations Φ(A)=const\Phi(A)=\mathrm{const}Φ(A)=const with Φ\PhiΦ continuous, and solution sets of continuous equations are closed.

Proposition 8.4 (The classical groups are matrix Lie groups). GL(n,R)\GL(n,\R)GL(n,R), SL(n,R)\SL(n,\R)SL(n,R), SL(n,C)\SL(n,\C)SL(n,C), O(n)\Orth(n)O(n), SO(n)\SO(n)SO(n), U(n)\U(n)U(n) and SU(n)\SU(n)SU(n) are matrix Lie groups.

Proof. Each is a subgroup (Lecture 1), cut out of GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C) by conditions among Im⁡A=0\operatorname{Im}A=0ImA=0, ATA=1A^{\mathsf T}A=\mathbb 1ATA=1, A†A=1A^{\dagger}A=\mathbb 1A†A=1, det⁡A=1\det A=1detA=1: finitely many closed conditions. 

Two new members join the zoo; both are previews.

Example 8.5 (The Lorentz group). With η=diag⁡(1,−1,−1,−1)\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)η=diag(1,−1,−1,−1), the Lorentz group O(1,3)={Λ∈GL(4,R):ΛTηΛ=η}\Orth(1,3)=\{\Lambda\in\GL(4,\R) : \Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta\}O(1,3)={Λ∈GL(4,R):ΛTηΛ=η} consists of the linear maps preserving the Minkowski form t2−x2−y2−z2t^2-x^2-y^2-z^2t2−x2−y2−z2; it is a matrix Lie group by the same pattern. Unlike its Euclidean cousin O(4)\Orth(4)O(4) it is unbounded, containing for every χ∈R\chi\in\Rχ∈R the boost Λ(χ)=(cosh⁡χsinh⁡χsinh⁡χcosh⁡χ)⊕12\Lambda(\chi)=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\cosh\chi&\sinh\chi\\ \sinh\chi&\cosh\chi\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\oplus\mathbb 1_{2}Λ(χ)=(coshχsinhχ​sinhχcoshχ​)⊕12​. Lecture 14 is devoted to this group.

Example 8.6 (The Heisenberg group). The Heisenberg group H3H_3H3​ of unitriangular matrices (1ac01b001)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&a&c\\0&1&b\\0&0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)(100​a10​cb1​), a,b,c∈Ra,b,c\in\Ra,b,c∈R, is closed (fixed entries are closed conditions) and unbounded. Multiplication adds the parameters a,ba,ba,b but twists the corner, c↦c+c′+ab′c\mapsto c+c'+ab'c↦c+c′+ab′: here, Lecture 13 will show, hide the canonical commutation relations of quantum mechanics. Note the device — translations made matrix-shaped by padding a dimension — reused in Lectures 13 and 15. (The symplectic family enters on Sheet 8 via Sp(2,R)=SL(2,R)\Sp(2,\R)=\SL(2,\R)Sp(2,R)=SL(2,R).)

Example 8.7 (SU(2)\SU(2)SU(2) is a sphere). For U∈SU(2)U\in\SU(2)U∈SU(2), det⁡U=1\det U=1detU=1 makes the inverse the adjugate; equating it with U†U^{\dagger}U† entry by entry leaves SU(2)={(αβ−βˉαˉ):α,β∈C, ∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1}, \SU(2)=\left\{ \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & \beta\\ -\bar\beta & \bar\alpha\end{pmatrix} : \alpha,\beta\in\C,\ \abs{\alpha}^2+\abs{\beta}^2=1\right\}, SU(2)={(α−βˉ​​βαˉ​):α,β∈C, ∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1}, the unit sphere S3S^3S3 in C2≅R4\C^2\cong\R^4C2≅R4: compact at a glance, connected, and — being a sphere — without holes that a loop could detect, a property Lecture 9 will name simply connected and exploit heavily.

Proposition 8.8 (Compactness in the zoo). O(n)\Orth(n)O(n), SO(n)\SO(n)SO(n), U(n)\U(n)U(n), SU(n)\SU(n)SU(n) are compact; GL\GLGL and SL\SLSL over R\RR or C\CC (for n≥2n\ge 2n≥2), O(1,3)\Orth(1,3)O(1,3) and H3H_3H3​ are not.

Proof. A unitary preserves lengths, so ∥U∥=1\norm{U}=1∥U∥=1: U(n)\U(n)U(n) is bounded; and it is closed in all of Mn(C)M_n(\C)Mn​(C), since A†A=1A^{\dagger}A=\mathbb 1A†A=1 is a closed condition that itself forces invertibility. Closed and bounded means compact, and O(n)\Orth(n)O(n), SO(n)\SO(n)SO(n), SU(n)\SU(n)SU(n) are closed subsets of U(n)\U(n)U(n). For the rest, unbounded families: diag⁡(t,1/t,1,…,1)\operatorname{diag}(t,1/t,1,\dots,1)diag(t,1/t,1,…,1), the boosts Λ(χ)\Lambda(\chi)Λ(χ), and a→∞a\to\inftya→∞ in H3H_3H3​. 

Compactness will become a load-bearing wall in Lecture 12: it is what lets Part I’s averaging trick survive, with sums replaced by integrals. The other geographic feature is connectedness: a set is path-connected if any two of its points are joined by a continuous path inside it, connected if it admits no partition into two nonempty relatively open pieces; paths imply connectedness (analysis), and the converse for matrix Lie groups falls out of Section 8.5.

Proposition 8.9 (O(n)\Orth(n)O(n) is disconnected). O(n)\Orth(n)O(n) is not connected; nor is GL(n,R)\GL(n,\R)GL(n,R).

Proof. On O(n)\Orth(n)O(n), (det⁡A)2=1(\det A)^2=1(detA)2=1 and the continuous det⁡\detdet attains both values ±1\pm 1±1 (at 1\mathbb 11 and at diag⁡(−1,1,…,1)\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,\dots,1)diag(−1,1,…,1)): the sets {det⁡=±1}\{\det=\pm 1\}{det=±1} are nonempty, open in O(n)\Orth(n)O(n), and partition it. For GL(n,R)\GL(n,\R)GL(n,R), use the sign of det⁡\detdet. 

So O(n)\Orth(n)O(n) splits into SO(n)\SO(n)SO(n) and its reflection coset — the continuous shadow of the rotation/reflection split in Lecture 1’s dihedral groups. The positive assertions will be earned: U(n)\U(n)U(n), SU(n)\SU(n)SU(n), SO(n)\SO(n)SO(n) in Section 8.5; GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C), SL(n,C)\SL(n,\C)SL(n,C), SL(n,R)\SL(n,\R)SL(n,R) on Sheet 8; the Lorentz group has exactly four pieces (Lecture 14) — why parity and time reversal are discrete choices, not limits of rotations.

Remark 8.10 (Abstract Lie groups). The wider literature defines a Lie group as a group that is also a smooth manifold — geometry we have not assumed. Nothing is lost: by a theorem of É. Cartan every closed subgroup of GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C) is such an object, and almost every Lie group of physical relevance is a matrix group or a quotient of one (the universal cover of SL(2,R)\SL(2,\R)SL(2,R) is the standard exception). Here, “Lie group” means matrix Lie group.

The matrix exponential

The tool that turns linear data into group elements is the oldest function in analysis, promoted to matrices.

Definition 8.11 (Matrix exponential). For X∈Mn(C)X\in M_n(\C)X∈Mn​(C), eX=exp⁡X=∑k=0∞Xkk!. e^{X}=\exp X=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{X^{k}}{k!} . eX=expX=k=0∑∞​k!Xk​.

Example 8.13 (The circle, twice). Let J=(0−110)J=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)J=(01​−10​), so J2=−1J^{2}=-\mathbb 1J2=−1 and the even/odd split of the series gives eθJ=cos⁡θ 1+sin⁡θ J=(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ)=R(θ):e^{\theta J} =\cos\theta\,\mathbb 1+\sin\theta\,J =\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix} =R(\theta):eθJ=cosθ1+sinθJ=(cosθsinθ​−sinθcosθ​)=R(θ): all of SO(2)\SO(2)SO(2) flows out of the single matrix JJJ. Theorem 8.15 (Spectral mapping; determinant and trace). If XXX has eigenvalues λ1,…,λn\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_nλ1​,…,λn​ (with multiplicity), then eXe^{X}eX has eigenvalues eλ1,…,eλne^{\lambda_1},\dots,e^{\lambda_n}eλ1​,…,eλn​, and det⁡eX=etr⁡X. \det e^{X}=e^{\tr X}. deteX=etrX.

Remark 8.18 (A first miracle, and a preview of Stone). Mere continuity forced analyticity — continuous symmetry is automatically differentiable symmetry, the matrix-sized shadow of Hilbert’s fifth problem. The infinite-dimensional sibling, Stone’s theorem (U(t)=e−itAU(t)=e^{-\ii tA}U(t)=e−itA, AAA self-adjoint), runs quantum time evolution and is quoted in Lecture 9; ours is its finite-dimensional case, the licence to speak of the generator of a continuous symmetry.

A nonzero one-parameter generator can act on space in sharply different ways. On the plane, the nonzero elements of sl(2,R)\sllie(2,\R)sl(2,R) fall into three qualitative generator/flow types — rotations, squeezes, and shears — fixed by the eigenvalues of XXX (Figure 8.2); the zero generator gives the stationary identity flow. This is not a claim that there are only three conjugacy classes of elements or subgroups; exceptional parameter values and sign/orientation data must also be retained. The squeezes return as Lorentz boosts in Lecture 14.

Theorem 8.19 (Lie product formula). For all X,Y∈Mn(C)X,Y\in M_n(\C)X,Y∈Mn​(C), eX+Y=lim⁡m→∞(eX/m eY/m)m\displaystyle e^{X+Y}=\lim_{m\to\infty}\Bigl(e^{X/m}\,e^{Y/m}\Bigr)^{m}eX+Y=m→∞lim​(eX/meY/m)m.

Proof. Multiplying series, eX/meY/m=1+X+Ym+Rme^{X/m}e^{Y/m}=\mathbb 1+\frac{X+Y}{m}+R_meX/meY/m=1+mX+Y​+Rm​ with ∥Rm∥≤c/m2\norm{R_m}\le c/m^{2}∥Rm​∥≤c/m2, c=c(X,Y)c=c(X,Y)c=c(X,Y): every term of combined degree d≥2d\ge 2d≥2 carries m−dm^{-d}m−d, with coefficients dominated by those of e∥X∥e∥Y∥e^{\norm{X}}e^{\norm{Y}}e∥X∥e∥Y∥. For large mmm this lies in the domain of log⁡\loglog, and the tail estimate ∥log⁡(1+B)−B∥≤∥B∥2\norm{\log(\mathbb 1+B)-B}\le\norm{B}^{2}∥log(1+B)−B∥≤∥B∥2 for ∥B∥≤12\norm{B}\le\tfrac12∥B∥≤21​ gives log⁡(eX/meY/m)=X+Ym+Sm\log(e^{X/m}e^{Y/m})=\frac{X+Y}{m}+S_mlog(eX/meY/m)=mX+Y​+Sm​ with ∥Sm∥≤c′/m2\norm{S_m}\le c'/m^{2}∥Sm​∥≤c′/m2. Hence, by (eZ)m=emZ(e^{Z})^{m}=e^{mZ}(eZ)m=emZ and continuity of exp⁡\expexp, (eX/meY/m)m=exp⁡(X+Y+mSm)→m→∞eX+Y.\Bigl(e^{X/m}e^{Y/m}\Bigr)^{m} =\exp\bigl(X+Y+mS_m\bigr) \xrightarrow[m\to\infty]{}e^{X+Y}.(eX/meY/m)m=exp(X+Y+mSm​)m→∞​eX+Y. 

(The formula is modern technology: alternating many short steps of e−itH1e^{-\ii tH_1}e−itH1​ and e−itH2e^{-\ii tH_2}e−itH2​ is how quantum simulators enact e−it(H1+H2)e^{-\ii t(H_1+H_2)}e−it(H1​+H2​), at the O(1/m)O(1/m)O(1/m) rate visible in the proof.)

The Lie algebra of a matrix Lie group

Here is the central definition of Part II. It asks of a matrix not where it is, but where it can take you.

Definition 8.20 (Lie algebra of a matrix Lie group). The Lie algebra of a matrix Lie group G⊆GL(n,C)G\subseteq\GL(n,\C)G⊆GL(n,C) is g=Lie⁡(G)={X∈Mn(C):etX∈G for all t∈R},\glie=\Lie(G)=\bigl\{X\in M_n(\C) : e^{tX}\in G\ \text{for all } t\in\R\bigr\},g=Lie(G)={X∈Mn​(C):etX∈G for all t∈R}, the set of matrices whose entire one-parameter flow stays inside GGG. Lie algebras wear fraktur: Lie⁡(SU(n))=su(n)\Lie(\SU(n))=\su(n)Lie(SU(n))=su(n), and so on.

Note the real parameter ttt, whatever the field of the matrices — a deliberate choice sorted out in Section 8.6. Physicists call elements of g\glieg infinitesimal generators; Corollary 8.32 will justify the name. Since every exponential is invertible, gl(n,C)=Mn(C)\gllie(n,\C)=M_n(\C)gl(n,C)=Mn​(C) and gl(n,R)=Mn(R)\gllie(n,\R)=M_n(\R)gl(n,R)=Mn​(R): no condition at all. For the rest, one two-step pattern does everything: differentiate the defining constraint at t=0t=0t=0 for necessity, exponentiate the linearised constraint for sufficiency.

Example 8.21 (sl\slliesl: trace zero). X∈sl(n,C)X\in\sllie(n,\C)X∈sl(n,C) means det⁡etX=ettr⁡X=1\det e^{tX}=e^{t\tr X}=1detetX=ettrX=1 for all ttt (8.5), i.e. tr⁡X=0\tr X=0trX=0 (differentiate at t=0t=0t=0); the converse is immediate. So sl(n,C)={X:tr⁡X=0}\sllie(n,\C)=\{X:\tr X=0\}sl(n,C)={X:trX=0}, likewise sl(n,R)\sllie(n,\R)sl(n,R) over R\RR.

Example 8.22 (u\ulieu and su\susu: anti-Hermitian). X∈u(n)X\in\ulie(n)X∈u(n) means (etX)†etX=etX†etX=1(e^{tX})^{\dagger}e^{tX}=e^{tX^{\dagger}}e^{tX}=\mathbb 1(etX)†etX=etX†etX=1 for all ttt; the derivative at t=0t=0t=0 (product rule, Proposition 8.12(v)) forces X†+X=0X^{\dagger}+X=0X†+X=0, and conversely X†=−XX^{\dagger}=-XX†=−X gives (etX)†etX=e−tXetX=1(e^{tX})^{\dagger}e^{tX}=e^{-tX}e^{tX}=\mathbb 1(etX)†etX=e−tXetX=1. So u(n)\ulie(n)u(n) is the space of anti-Hermitian matrices and su(n)={X†=−X, tr⁡X=0}\su(n)=\{X^{\dagger}=-X,\ \tr X=0\}su(n)={X†=−X, trX=0}. Counting real parameters (imaginary diagonal, free complex entries above it) gives dim⁡Ru(n)=n2\dim_{\R}\ulie(n)=n^{2}dimR​u(n)=n2 and, the trace here being one real condition, dim⁡Rsu(n)=n2−1\dim_{\R}\su(n)=n^{2}-1dimR​su(n)=n2−1. For n=1n=1n=1: u(1)=iR\ulie(1)=\ii\Ru(1)=iR, the tangent line of Figure 8.1.

Example 8.23 (so\soso: antisymmetric — and blind). The same computation with T\mathsf TT for †\dagger† gives Lie⁡(O(n))={X∈Mn(R):XT=−X}\Lie(\Orth(n))=\{X\in M_n(\R) : X^{\mathsf T}=-X\}Lie(O(n))={X∈Mn​(R):XT=−X}, of dimension n(n−1)/2n(n-1)/2n(n−1)/2. An antisymmetric matrix has zero diagonal, so tr⁡X=0\tr X=0trX=0 is automatic and the determinant condition adds nothing: Lie⁡(O(n))=Lie⁡(SO(n))=so(n)\Lie(\Orth(n))=\Lie(\SO(n))=\so(n)Lie(O(n))=Lie(SO(n))=so(n). The algebra cannot tell O(n)\Orth(n)O(n) from SO(n)\SO(n)SO(n) — a moral, not an accident: differentiation at the identity sees only the connected piece containing it — SO(n)\SO(n)SO(n), never the reflections.

Example 8.24 (The Lorentz algebra). For O(1,3)\Orth(1,3)O(1,3) the constraint (etX)Tη etX=η(e^{tX})^{\mathsf T}\eta\,e^{tX}=\eta(etX)TηetX=η linearises to XTη+ηX=0X^{\mathsf T}\eta+\eta X=0XTη+ηX=0, i.e. ηX\eta XηX antisymmetric: in 1+31{+}31+3 block form, X=(0b⃗Tb⃗A)X=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&\vec b^{\,\mathsf T}\\ \vec b&A\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)X=(0b​bTA​) with b⃗∈R3\vec b\in\R^3b∈R3 free and AT=−AA^{\mathsf T}=-AAT=−A, so dim⁡Rso(1,3)=3+3=6\dim_{\R}\so(1,3)=3+3=6dimR​so(1,3)=3+3=6: three boosts (b⃗\vec bb, symmetric placement), three rotations (AAA, antisymmetric). How profoundly the two triples differ is Lecture 14’s business.

Example 8.25 (The Heisenberg algebra). For H3H_3H3​, exponentials of strictly upper triangular XXX truncate to unitriangular polynomials, and differentiating the fixed entries of etXe^{tX}etX at t=0t=0t=0 forces the converse: h3\mathfrak h_3h3​ is the three-dimensional space of strictly upper triangular matrices, with [X,X′]=(ab′−a′b)E13[X,X']=(ab'-a'b)E_{13}[X,X′]=(ab′−a′b)E13​ — every commutator points along the corner entry, which commutes with everything: the shadow of [q^,p^]=iℏ[\hat q,\hat p]=\ii\hbar[q^​,p^​]=iℏ (Lecture 13).

So far g\glieg is only a set. The next theorem gives it its structure — and reveals why the definition of a matrix Lie group insisted on closedness.

Theorem 8.26 (g\glieg is closed under sums, conjugation, commutators). Let GGG be a matrix Lie group with Lie algebra g\glieg. Then

  1. g\glieg is a real vector subspace of Mn(C)M_n(\C)Mn​(C);

  2. gXg−1∈ggXg^{-1}\in\gliegXg−1∈g for all g∈Gg\in Gg∈G, X∈gX\in\glieX∈g;

Proof. (i) et(sX)=e(ts)X∈Ge^{t(sX)}=e^{(ts)X}\in Get(sX)=e(ts)X∈G handles real multiples. For sums, the Lie product formula gives et(X+Y)=lim⁡m(etX/m etY/m)me^{t(X+Y)}=\lim_{m}\bigl(e^{tX/m}\,e^{tY/m}\bigr)^{m}et(X+Y)=limm​(etX/metY/m)m: every matrix under the limit lies in GGG, the limit is invertible (an exponential), and GGG is closed in GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C) — so et(X+Y)∈Ge^{t(X+Y)}\in Get(X+Y)∈G for all ttt, i.e. X+Y∈gX+Y\in\glieX+Y∈g. Here the closedness hypothesis earns its keep; it will once more, in Theorem 8.31.

(ii) et(gXg−1)=g etXg−1∈Ge^{t(gXg^{-1})}=g\,e^{tX}g^{-1}\in Get(gXg−1)=getXg−1∈G (Proposition 8.12(ii)).

(iii) By (ii), the curve Z(t)=etXYe−tXZ(t)=e^{tX}Ye^{-tX}Z(t)=etXYe−tX lies in g\glieg for all ttt; by (i), g\glieg is a finite-dimensional real subspace of Mn(C)M_n(\C)Mn​(C), hence a closed subset. The difference quotients (Z(t)−Z(0))/t(Z(t)-Z(0))/t(Z(t)−Z(0))/t lie in g\glieg and converge (product rule) to Z′(0)=XY−YX=[X,Y]Z'(0)=XY-YX=[X,Y]Z′(0)=XY−YX=[X,Y], which therefore lies in g\glieg. 

The bracket [X,Y][X,Y][X,Y] measures noncommutativity to first order; that it never leads out of g\glieg is the linearised residue of GGG being closed under multiplication. The structure deserves axioms.

Definition 8.27 (Lie algebra; homomorphism). A Lie algebra over R\RR (or C\CC) is a real (complex) vector space g\glieg with a bracket [⋅ ,⋅] ⁣:g×g→g[\cdot\,,\cdot]\colon\glie\times\glie\to\glie[⋅,⋅]:g×g→g, bilinear, antisymmetric, and satisfying the Jacobi identity [X,[Y,Z]]+[Y,[Z,X]]+[Z,[X,Y]]=0.\bigl[X,[Y,Z]\bigr]+\bigl[Y,[Z,X]\bigr]+\bigl[Z,[X,Y]\bigr]=0 .[X,[Y,Z]]+[Y,[Z,X]]+[Z,[X,Y]]=0. A linear map with φ([X,Y])=[φ(X),φ(Y)]\varphi([X,Y])=[\varphi(X),\varphi(Y)]φ([X,Y])=[φ(X),φ(Y)] is a homomorphism of Lie algebras, a bijective one an isomorphism (≅\cong≅). Relative to a basis X1,…,XdX_1,\dots,X_dX1​,…,Xd​, the structure constants fabcf_{ab}{}^{c}fab​c defined by [Xa,Xb]=fabcXc[X_a,X_b]=f_{ab}{}^{c}X_c[Xa​,Xb​]=fab​cXc​ (sum over ccc) pin the algebra down completely.

The matrix commutator is bilinear and antisymmetric, and the twelve terms of its Jacobi identity cancel in pairs upon expansion: every Lie⁡(G)\Lie(G)Lie(G) is a real Lie algebra in the abstract sense.

Example 8.28 (su(2)\su(2)su(2) and so(3)\so(3)so(3)). Two three-dimensional specimens will dominate the next four lectures. [X_j,X_k] =-\tfrac{1}{4}[\sigma_j,\sigma_k] =\epsilon_{jkl}\,X_l . [Xj​,Xk​]=−41​[σj​,σk​]=ϵjkl​Xl​. In so(3)\so(3)so(3), for ω⃗∈R3\vec\omega\in\R^{3}ω∈R3 let ω^\hat\omegaω^ have entries (ω^)jk=−ϵajkωa(\hat\omega)_{jk}=-\epsilon_{ajk}\omega_a(ω^)jk​=−ϵajk​ωa​, so that ω^ x⃗=ω⃗×x⃗\hat\omega\,\vec x=\vec\omega\times\vec xω^x=ω×x: the hat map ω⃗↦ω^\vec\omega\mapsto\hat\omegaω↦ω^ is a linear bijection R3→so(3)\R^{3}\to\so(3)R3→so(3) (both have dimension 333), and the basis La=e^aL_a=\hat e_aLa​=e^a​ generates the rotations about the axes — eθL3e^{\theta L_3}eθL3​ is Example 8.13’s R(θ)R(\theta)R(θ) in the xyxyxy-plane.

Proposition 8.29 (One algebra, three costumes). The hat map and the assignment Xa↦LaX_a\mapsto L_aXa​↦La​ are Lie algebra isomorphisms (R3,×)  ≅  so(3)  ≅  su(2).\bigl(\R^{3},\times\bigr)\;\cong\;\so(3)\;\cong\;\su(2).(R3,×)≅so(3)≅su(2).

Proof. The cross product is bilinear, antisymmetric, and its Jacobi identity is the classical identity a⃗×(b⃗×c⃗)+b⃗×(c⃗×a⃗)+c⃗×(a⃗×b⃗)=0\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)+\vec b\times(\vec c\times\vec a) +\vec c\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=0a×(b×c)+b×(c×a)+c×(a×b)=0. The same identity, applied to a vector x⃗\vec xx, evaluates the matrix commutator: [ω^,ν^] x⃗=ω⃗×(ν⃗×x⃗)−ν⃗×(ω⃗×x⃗)=(ω⃗×ν⃗)×x⃗,[\hat\omega,\hat\nu]\,\vec x =\vec\omega\times(\vec\nu\times\vec x) -\vec\nu\times(\vec\omega\times\vec x) =(\vec\omega\times\vec\nu)\times\vec x ,[ω^,ν^]x=ω×(ν×x)−ν×(ω×x)=(ω×ν)×x, so [ω^,ν^]=ω⃗×ν⃗^[\hat\omega,\hat\nu]=\widehat{\vec\omega\times\vec\nu}[ω^,ν^]=ω×ν​ and the hat map preserves brackets. In particular [Lj,Lk]=ej×ek^=ϵjklLl[L_j,L_k]=\widehat{e_j\times e_k}=\epsilon_{jkl}L_l[Lj​,Lk​]=ej​×ek​​=ϵjkl​Ll​ — the structure constants (8.6) — so Xa↦LaX_a\mapsto L_aXa​↦La​ extends to an isomorphism too. 

Remark 8.30 (The algebra is short-sighted). So su(2)≅so(3)\su(2)\cong\so(3)su(2)≅so(3), yet the groups are not isomorphic: SU(2)\SU(2)SU(2) is the sphere S3S^{3}S3 of Example 8.7, while SO(3)\SO(3)SO(3), Lecture 11 will show, is that sphere with antipodes glued — with consequences the size of the electron’s spin. Together with Lie⁡(O(n))=Lie⁡(SO(n))\Lie(\Orth(n))=\Lie(\SO(n))Lie(O(n))=Lie(SO(n)), this calibrates how much the algebra remembers: everything near the identity, nothing global.

The exponential as a bridge

By construction exp⁡\expexp maps g\glieg into GGG, and by Theorem 8.16 it is injective near 000. What is not obvious — and is the deepest statement of this lecture — is that near the identity it fills GGG: a closed subgroup of GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C) has no elements loitering near 1\mathbb 11 other than exponentials of its own Lie algebra.

Theorem 8.31 (Exponential coordinates). Let GGG be a matrix Lie group with Lie algebra g\glieg. There exist ε∈(0,log⁡2)\varepsilon\in(0,\log 2)ε∈(0,log2) and a neighbourhood VVV of 1\mathbb 11 in GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C) such that every g∈G∩Vg\in G\cap Vg∈G∩V is g=eXg=e^{X}g=eX for a unique X∈gX\in\glieX∈g with ∥X∥<ε\norm{X}<\varepsilon∥X∥<ε.

Proof. Choose a real subspace DDD with Mn(C)=g⊕DM_n(\C)=\glie\oplus DMn​(C)=g⊕D and define φ ⁣:g×D→GL(n,C)\varphi\colon\glie\times D\to\GL(n,\C)φ:g×D→GL(n,C), φ(X,Y)=eXeY\varphi(X,Y)=e^{X}e^{Y}φ(X,Y)=eXeY — smooth (convergent power series), with φ(X,Y)=1+X+Y+(higher order)\varphi(X,Y)=\mathbb 1+X+Y+(\text{higher order})φ(X,Y)=1+X+Y+(higher order), so its derivative at (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) is (X,Y)↦X+Y(X,Y)\mapsto X+Y(X,Y)↦X+Y, a linear bijection onto Mn(C)M_n(\C)Mn​(C). By the inverse function theorem (Remark 8.3) there are δ>0\delta>0δ>0 and a neighbourhood V0V_0V0​ of 1\mathbb 11 in which every ggg factors uniquely as g=eXeYg=e^{X}e^{Y}g=eXeY, X∈gX\in\glieX∈g, Y∈DY\in DY∈D, ∥X∥,∥Y∥<δ\norm{X},\norm{Y}<\delta∥X∥,∥Y∥<δ, the factors depending continuously on ggg. It remains to show that for g∈Gg\in Gg∈G near 1\mathbb 11 the second factor vanishes. Suppose not: there are gm∈Gg_m\in Ggm​∈G, gm→1g_m\to\mathbb 1gm​→1, with gm=eXmeYmg_m=e^{X_m}e^{Y_m}gm​=eXm​eYm​, Ym≠0Y_m\neq 0Ym​=0, and Xm,Ym→0X_m,Y_m\to 0Xm​,Ym​→0 by continuity; since eXm∈Ge^{X_m}\in GeXm​∈G, also eYm=e−Xmgm∈Ge^{Y_m}=e^{-X_m}g_m\in GeYm​=e−Xm​gm​∈G. The unit vectors Ym/∥Ym∥Y_m/\norm{Y_m}Ym​/∥Ym​∥ live on the unit sphere of DDD, which is compact; after passing to a subsequence, Ym/∥Ym∥→Y∈DY_m/\norm{Y_m}\to Y\in DYm​/∥Ym​∥→Y∈D, ∥Y∥=1\norm{Y}=1∥Y∥=1. Fix t∈Rt\in\Rt∈R and let kmk_mkm​ be the integer nearest t/∥Ym∥t/\norm{Y_m}t/∥Ym​∥, so km∥Ym∥→tk_m\norm{Y_m}\to tkm​∥Ym​∥→t (rounding error ≤∥Ym∥→0\le\norm{Y_m}\to 0≤∥Ym​∥→0); then (eYm)km=exp⁡(km∥Ym∥ Ym∥Ym∥)→m→∞etY.\bigl(e^{Y_m}\bigr)^{k_m} =\exp\Bigl(k_m\norm{Y_m}\,\tfrac{Y_m}{\norm{Y_m}}\Bigr) \xrightarrow[m\to\infty]{}e^{tY}.(eYm​)km​=exp(km​∥Ym​∥∥Ym​∥Ym​​)m→∞​etY. Corollary 8.32 (Generators are velocities). g\glieg consists exactly of the velocities γ′(0)\gamma'(0)γ′(0) of the curves γ ⁣:(−δ,δ)→G\gamma\colon(-\delta,\delta)\to Gγ:(−δ,δ)→G that are differentiable at 000 with γ(0)=1\gamma(0)=\mathbb 1γ(0)=1.

Proof. (⊆\subseteq⊆) XXX is the velocity of etXe^{tX}etX. (⊇\supseteq⊇) For small ttt, Theorem 8.31 writes γ(t)=eZ(t)\gamma(t)=e^{Z(t)}γ(t)=eZ(t), Z(t)=log⁡γ(t)∈gZ(t)=\log\gamma(t)\in\glieZ(t)=logγ(t)∈g; with A=γ′(0)A=\gamma'(0)A=γ′(0), the tail estimate ∥log⁡(1+B)−B∥≤∥B∥2\norm{\log(\mathbb 1+B)-B}\le\norm{B}^{2}∥log(1+B)−B∥≤∥B∥2 gives Z(t)=tA+o(t)Z(t)=tA+o(t)Z(t)=tA+o(t), so Z(t)/t→AZ(t)/t\to AZ(t)/t→A inside the closed subspace g\glieg. 

The corollary is why “infinitesimal generator” is honest language — and mechanics has used it all along: for a rigid-body attitude t↦R(t)∈SO(3)t\mapsto R(t)\in\SO(3)t↦R(t)∈SO(3), the curve t↦R(s+t)R(s)−1t\mapsto R(s+t)R(s)^{-1}t↦R(s+t)R(s)−1 passes through 1\mathbb 11, so R˙(s)R(s)−1=ω^(s)∈so(3)\dot R(s)R(s)^{-1}=\hat\omega(s)\in\so(3)R˙(s)R(s)−1=ω^(s)∈so(3) and body points obey x⃗˙=ω⃗×x⃗\dot{\vec x}=\vec\omega\times\vec xx˙=ω×x: the angular velocity vector is a Lie algebra element, named in mechanics before its time.

How much of GGG does exp⁡\expexp reach beyond a neighbourhood of 1\mathbb 11? Exactly the part connected to it. Write G0G^{0}G0 for the identity component of GGG: the set of g∈Gg\in Gg∈G joined to 1\mathbb 11 by some continuous path in GGG.

Theorem 8.33 (The identity component). G0G^{0}G0 is a normal subgroup of GGG, and G0={eX1⋯eXk:k∈N, Xi∈g}G^{0}=\{e^{X_1}\cdots e^{X_k} : k\in\N,\ X_i\in\glie\}G0={eX1​⋯eXk​:k∈N, Xi​∈g}.

Proof. If γg,γh\gamma_g,\gamma_hγg​,γh​ join 1\mathbb 11 to g,hg,hg,h, then γgγh\gamma_g\gamma_hγg​γh​ joins it to ghghgh and γg−1\gamma_g^{-1}γg−1​ to g−1g^{-1}g−1: G0G^{0}G0 is a subgroup; conjugation by any a∈Ga\in Ga∈G is continuous and fixes 1\mathbb 11, hence permutes such paths: aG0a−1=G0aG^{0}a^{-1}=G^{0}aG0a−1=G0.

Let PPP be the set of finite products of exponentials — a subgroup, since (eX)−1=e−X(e^{X})^{-1}=e^{-X}(eX)−1=e−X. Shrinking the factors, t↦etX1⋯etXkt\mapsto e^{tX_1}\cdots e^{tX_k}t↦etX1​⋯etXk​ is a path from 1\mathbb 11, so P⊆G0P\subseteq G^{0}P⊆G0. Conversely, W=G∩VW=G\cap VW=G∩V of Theorem 8.31 satisfies W⊆exp⁡(g)⊆PW\subseteq\exp(\glie)\subseteq PW⊆exp(g)⊆P and is a neighbourhood of 1\mathbb 11 in GGG; for p∈Pp\in Pp∈P, pWpWpW is a neighbourhood of ppp contained in PPP, so PPP is open in GGG; each coset aPaPaP is open, so the complement of PPP (a union of cosets) is open too. PPP is thus open and closed in GGG; since G0G^{0}G0 is connected and meets PPP in 1\mathbb 11, G0⊆PG^{0}\subseteq PG0⊆P. 

Corollary 8.34. A connected matrix Lie group is path-connected and is generated by any neighbourhood of its identity. G0G^{0}G0 is itself a matrix Lie group with Lie⁡(G0)=g\Lie(G^{0})=\glieLie(G0)=g, and G/G0G/G^{0}G/G0 is the group of components: e.g. det⁡ ⁣:O(n)→{±1}\det\colon\Orth(n)\to\{\pm 1\}det:O(n)→{±1} has kernel SO(n)=O(n)0\SO(n)=\Orth(n)^{0}SO(n)=O(n)0, so O(n)/SO(n)≅Z2\Orth(n)/\SO(n)\cong\Z_2O(n)/SO(n)≅Z2​ by Lecture 2’s first isomorphism theorem.

Proof. If GGG is connected the proof above gives G=PG=PG=P, with WWW shrunk into any given neighbourhood — the generation claim — and every element of PPP is path-connected to 1\mathbb 11. G0G^{0}G0 is closed in GGG (its complement is a union of cosets of an open subgroup), hence a matrix Lie group containing the flows etXe^{tX}etX: Lie⁡(G0)=g\Lie(G^{0})=\glieLie(G0)=g. The example is the first isomorphism theorem applied to det⁡\detdet. 

For the compact members of the zoo, the linear-algebra prerequisite upgrades “generated by exponentials” to “equal to the exponentials”.

Theorem 8.35 (Surjectivity for the unitary and rotation groups). exp⁡\expexp maps u(n)\ulie(n)u(n) onto U(n)\U(n)U(n), su(n)\su(n)su(n) onto SU(n)\SU(n)SU(n), and so(n)\so(n)so(n) onto SO(n)\SO(n)SO(n); consequently these three groups are (path-)connected.

Proof. U(n)\U(n)U(n): the spectral theorem (Remark 8.3) writes U=VDV†U=VDV^{\dagger}U=VDV† with VVV unitary and D=diag⁡(eiθ1,…,eiθn)D=\operatorname{diag}(e^{\ii\theta_1},\dots,e^{\ii\theta_n})D=diag(eiθ1​,…,eiθn​); then X=Vdiag⁡(iθj)V†X=V\operatorname{diag}(\ii\theta_j)V^{\dagger}X=Vdiag(iθj​)V† is anti-Hermitian with eX=Ue^{X}=UeX=U.

SU(n)\SU(n)SU(n): in addition det⁡U=ei∑θj=1\det U=e^{\ii\sum\theta_j}=1detU=ei∑θj​=1, so ∑jθj=2πk\sum_j\theta_j=2\pi k∑j​θj​=2πk; replacing θ1\theta_1θ1​ by θ1−2πk\theta_1-2\pi kθ1​−2πk changes neither eiθ1e^{\ii\theta_1}eiθ1​ nor UUU and puts XXX in su(n)\su(n)su(n).

SO(n)\SO(n)SO(n): the normal form for special orthogonal matrices (Remark 8.3) writes R=QBQTR=QBQ^{\mathsf T}R=QBQT with Q∈O(n)Q\in\Orth(n)Q∈O(n) and B=blockdiag⁡(R(θ1),…,R(θm),1)B=\operatorname{blockdiag}\bigl(R(\theta_1),\dots,R(\theta_m), \mathbb 1\bigr)B=blockdiag(R(θ1​),…,R(θm​),1): eigenvalue pairs e±iθe^{\pm\ii\theta}e±iθ give rotation blocks, and the eigenvalue −1-1−1, occurring an even number of times since det⁡R=1\det R=1detR=1, pairs into blocks R(π)R(\pi)R(π). Then X=Qblockdiag⁡(θ1J,…,θmJ,0)QTX=Q\operatorname{blockdiag}\bigl(\theta_1J,\dots,\theta_mJ,0\bigr) Q^{\mathsf T}X=Qblockdiag(θ1​J,…,θm​J,0)QT is antisymmetric with eX=Re^{X}=ReX=R, by Example 8.13 applied blockwise.

Connectedness: t↦etXt\mapsto e^{tX}t↦etX is a path from 1\mathbb 11 to eXe^{X}eX inside the group. 

This settles three “yes” entries of Table 8.1: for these groups one exponential suffices in Theorem 8.33 — a luxury of compactness, not a law:

Example 8.36 (exp⁡\expexp need not be surjective). A=(−110−1)∈SL(2,C)A=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&1\\0&-1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) \in\SL(2,\C)A=(−10​1−1​)∈SL(2,C) is no exponential of sl(2,C)\sllie(2,\C)sl(2,C): such an XXX has eigenvalues ±λ\pm\lambda±λ (their sum is tr⁡X=0\tr X=0trX=0), so eXe^{X}eX has eigenvalues e±λe^{\pm\lambda}e±λ, while both eigenvalues of AAA are −1-1−1: then λ∈iπ(2Z+1)\lambda\in\ii\pi(2\Z{+}1)λ∈iπ(2Z+1), so λ≠−λ\lambda\neq-\lambdaλ=−λ, XXX is diagonalisable, and so is eXe^{X}eX — but AAA, with one-dimensional (−1)(-1)(−1)-eigenspace, is not. Yet SL(2,C)\SL(2,\C)SL(2,C) is connected (Sheet 8), and two exponentials reach AAA: A=exp⁡(iπdiag⁡(1,−1))exp⁡(0−100)A=\exp\bigl(\ii\pi\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\bigr) \exp\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)A=exp(iπdiag(1,−1))exp(00​−10​), both exponents traceless, in keeping with Theorem 8.33.

Let us take stock. Locally the bridge is perfect: Theorems 8.16 and 8.31 say that near the identity GGG is g\glieg in curved coordinates; the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula (stated in Lecture 9) even expresses log⁡(eXeY)\log(e^{X}e^{Y})log(eXeY) in iterated brackets alone. Globally, three phenomena appeared: exp⁡\expexp can fail to be injective (the circle), can fail to be surjective (SL(2,C)\SL(2,\C)SL(2,C)), and distinct groups can share one algebra (su(2)≅so(3)\su(2)\cong\so(3)su(2)≅so(3)). The first two are bookkeeping; the third is a door, and Lectures 9 and 11 walk through it. (Sheet 8 adds the polar decomposition of GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C), anatomy Lecture 14 will need.)

Real and complex Lie algebras, and the physicist’s conventions

One structural point was left deliberately loose, and physics conventions live in the slack. The Lie algebras of Definition 8.20 are real vector spaces — the flow parameter is real — even when their matrices are complex. Some are complex spaces too (gl(n,C)\gllie(n,\C)gl(n,C), sl(n,C)\sllie(n,\C)sl(n,C) are closed under multiplication by i\iii); the most important are not, since X†=−XX^{\dagger}=-XX†=−X gives (iX)†=+ iX(\ii X)^{\dagger}=+\,\ii X(iX)†=+iX: multiplying an anti-Hermitian matrix by i\iii produces a Hermitian one. “su(2)\su(2)su(2) consists of complex matrices” is not “su(2)\su(2)su(2) is a complex Lie algebra”. When complex scalars are wanted — Lecture 10 will want them badly — they must be adjoined by hand.

Definition 8.37 (Complexification). Let g⊆Mn(C)\glie\subseteq M_n(\C)g⊆Mn​(C) be a real Lie algebra of matrices with g∩ig={0}\glie\cap\ii\glie=\{0\}g∩ig={0}. Its complexification is the complex Lie algebra gC=g⊕ig={X+iY:X,Y∈g},\glie_{\C}=\glie\oplus\ii\glie =\{X+\ii Y : X,Y\in\glie\},gC​=g⊕ig={X+iY:X,Y∈g}, with the bracket extended by complex bilinearity. (For g\glieg already complex the recipe degenerates; the abstract g⊗RC\glie\otimes_{\R}\Cg⊗R​C then doubles the algebra — pedantry turned physics in Lecture 14, where complexifying so(1,3)\so(1,3)so(1,3) yields two commuting copies of sl(2,C)\sllie(2,\C)sl(2,C): the left/right labels on Weyl spinors.)

Proposition 8.38 (The classical complexifications). su(n)C=sl(n,C)\su(n)_{\C}=\sllie(n,\C)su(n)C​=sl(n,C), u(n)C=gl(n,C)\ulie(n)_{\C}=\gllie(n,\C)u(n)C​=gl(n,C), sl(n,R)C=sl(n,C)\sllie(n,\R)_{\C}=\sllie(n,\C)sl(n,R)C​=sl(n,C).

Proof. Anti-Hermitian ∩\cap∩ Hermitian ={0}=\{0\}={0} gives su(n)∩i su(n)={0}\su(n)\cap\ii\,\su(n)=\{0\}su(n)∩isu(n)={0}, and any traceless MMM splits as M=12(M−M†)⏟=:X+  i (−i2)(M+M†)⏟=:Y,M=\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(M-M^{\dagger}\bigr)}_{=:X} +\;\ii\,\underbrace{\bigl(-\tfrac{\ii}{2}\bigr) \bigl(M+M^{\dagger}\bigr)}_{=:Y},M==:X21​(M−M†)​​+i=:Y(−2i​)(M+M†)​​, with X,YX,YX,Y anti-Hermitian and traceless (as tr⁡M†=tr⁡M‾=0\tr M^{\dagger}=\overline{\tr M}=0trM†=trM=0): the first claim; dropping traces gives the second, real/imaginary parts the third. 

A complexification forgets information: different real algebras can share one. The pair that matters most in physics:

Proposition 8.39 (Two real forms of sl(2,C)\sllie(2,\C)sl(2,C)). su(2)C≅sl(2,R)C≅sl(2,C)\su(2)_{\C}\cong\sllie(2,\R)_{\C}\cong\sllie(2,\C)su(2)C​≅sl(2,R)C​≅sl(2,C), but su(2)≇sl(2,R)\su(2)\not\cong\sllie(2,\R)su(2)≅sl(2,R) as real Lie algebras.

Proof. The complexifications are Proposition 8.38; for the difference, equip su(2)\su(2)su(2) with the real inner product ⟨A,B⟩=−tr⁡(AB)\inner{A}{B}=-\tr(AB)⟨A,B⟩=−tr(AB); by cyclicity of the trace ⟨[X,A],B⟩+⟨A,[X,B]⟩=−tr⁡(XAB−ABX)=0\inner{[X,A]}{B}+\inner{A}{[X,B]}=-\tr(XAB-ABX)=0⟨[X,A],B⟩+⟨A,[X,B]⟩=−tr(XAB−ABX)=0, so every ad⁡X=[X,⋅ ]\ad_X=[X,\cdot\,]adX​=[X,⋅] is skew-symmetric and has purely imaginary eigenvalues (linear algebra). In sl(2,R)\sllie(2,\R)sl(2,R), by contrast, H=diag⁡(1,−1)H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)H=diag(1,−1) and the off-diagonal units E,FE,FE,F obey [H,E]=2E[H,E]=2E[H,E]=2E, [H,F]=−2F[H,F]=-2F[H,F]=−2F, so ad⁡H\ad_HadH​ has the real eigenvalues 2,−2,02,-2,02,−2,0. An isomorphism φ\varphiφ would intertwine ad⁡H\ad_HadH​ with ad⁡φ(H)\ad_{\varphi(H)}adφ(H)​, forcing real nonzero eigenvalues on an ad⁡\adad of su(2)\su(2)su(2) — impossible. 

Every ad⁡\adad skew versus some ad⁡\adad stretching: precisely Lecture 14’s contrast between rotations and boosts — one complex algebra, several real forms, different physics.

The physicist’s conventions

Physics texts populate su(n)\su(n)su(n) not with anti-Hermitian matrices but with Hermitian generators — Hermitian operators are observables. The translation is one factor of i\iii: for a basis X1,…,XdX_1,\dots,X_dX1​,…,Xd​ of g⊆u(n)\glie\subseteq\ulie(n)g⊆u(n) with real structure constants fabcf_{ab}{}^{c}fab​c, set Ta=iXaT_a=\ii X_aTa​=iXa​ (Hermitian); then eθaXa=e−iθaTa,[Ta,Tb]=−[Xa,Xb]=ifabc Tc: e^{\theta^{a}X_a}=e^{-\ii\theta^{a}T_a}, \qquad [T_a,T_b]=-[X_a,X_b]=\ii f_{ab}{}^{c}\,T_c : eθaXa​=e−iθaTa​,[Ta​,Tb​]=−[Xa​,Xb​]=ifab​cTc​: the mathematician’s (Xa,fabc)(X_a,f_{ab}{}^{c})(Xa​,fab​c) and the physicist’s (Ta,ifabc)(T_a,\ii f_{ab}{}^{c})(Ta​,ifab​c) are one structure in two fonts. The sign e−iθTe^{-\ii\theta T}e−iθT matches the quantum-mechanical e−itH/ℏe^{-\ii tH/\hbar}e−itH/ℏ and is fixed henceforth.

Example 8.40 (Angular momentum, before quantum mechanics). For su(2)\su(2)su(2) with Xa=−i2σaX_a=-\tfrac{\ii}{2}\sigma_aXa​=−2i​σa​, the Hermitian generators are Ja=12σaJ_a=\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma_aJa​=21​σa​, and (8.6), (8.4) become [Jj,Jk]=i ϵjkl Jl,e−iθ n⃗⋅J⃗=cos⁡θ2 1−isin⁡θ2 n⃗⋅σ⃗. [J_j,J_k]=\ii\,\epsilon_{jkl}\,J_l , \qquad e^{-\ii\theta\,\vec n\cdot\vec J} =\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,\mathbb 1 -\ii\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma . [Jj​,Jk​]=iϵjkl​Jl​,e−iθn⋅J=cos2θ​1−isin2θ​n⋅σ. The commutation relations of angular momentum, derived from the geometry of SU(2)\SU(2)SU(2) alone: Lecture 10 takes (8.8) as the seed from which the entire theory of spin grows.

Remark 8.41 (Where the Hermitian generators actually live). The real span ig\ii\glieig of the TaT_aTa​ is not bracket-closed ([iX,iY]=−[X,Y]∈g[\ii X,\ii Y]=-[X,Y]\in\glie[iX,iY]=−[X,Y]∈g — the stray i\iii in (8.7)): “the algebra of Hermitian generators” is shorthand for g\glieg or gC\glie_{\C}gC​, where XaX_aXa​, TaT_aTa​ and Lecture 10’s ladder operators σ±=12(σ1±iσ2)\sigma_{\pm}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\sigma_1\pm\ii\sigma_2)σ±​=21​(σ1​±iσ2​) all coexist. Complexify, and the bookkeeping dissolves.

The bridge is complete: groups, algebras, the exponential between. Lecture 9 sends Part I’s representations across it — differentiating, exponentiating back when topology permits, meeting Noether’s theorem where the directions touch physics; the rest of Part I survives once averaging becomes integration (Lecture 12).

Remark 8.42 (Computer algebra). The notebook computes exponentials by truncated series and by MatrixExp; checks eX∈SU(2)e^{X}\in\SU(2)eX∈SU(2) for random X∈su(2)X\in\su(2)X∈su(2); plots one-parameter orbits in SL(2,R)\SL(2,\R)SL(2,R) (ellipses, hyperbolas, shears — the flows of Figure 8.2, met again as boosts in Lecture 14); measures the O(1/m)O(1/m)O(1/m) Lie-product rate; and recovers so(3)\so(3)so(3)’s structure constants numerically.

Summary

  • Matrix Lie group. A closed subgroup of GL(n,C)\GL(n,\C)GL(n,C) (Definition 8.1); the classical groups qualify, with compactness and connectedness as catalogued (Proposition 8.4).
  • Matrix exponential. eX=∑kXk/k!e^{X}=\sum_k X^k/k!eX=∑k​Xk/k! with det⁡eX=etr⁡X\det e^{X}=e^{\tr X}deteX=etrX (Theorem 8.15), a local inverse to log⁡\loglog near the identity (Theorem 8.16).
  • One-parameter subgroups. Every continuous R→G\R\to GR→G has the form t↦etXt\mapsto e^{tX}t↦etX (Theorem 8.17); the Lie product formula rebuilds products from generators (Theorem 8.19).
  • Lie algebra. g={X:etX∈G ∀t}\glie=\{X:e^{tX}\in G\ \forall t\}g={X:etX∈G ∀t}, a real vector space closed under the commutator (Definition 8.20, Theorem 8.26); its elements are tangent velocities (Corollary 8.32).
  • Exponential and complexification. exp⁡\expexp is onto for U(n),SU(n),SO(n)\U(n),\SU(n),\SO(n)U(n),SU(n),SO(n) (Theorem 8.35); sl(2,C)\sllie(2,\C)sl(2,C) has real forms su(2)\su(2)su(2) and sl(2,R)\sllie(2,\R)sl(2,R) (Proposition 8.39); physics dictionary X=−iAX=-\ii AX=−iA, AAA Hermitian (eq. (8.7)).

Self-check

5 questions on the ideas this lecture is most often misread on. Answer before you look — a wrong answer you thought about is worth more than a right one you guessed.

1What geometric role does a Lie-algebra element play?

Differentiate a path through the identity.

Lie-algebra elements are the infinitesimal velocities of one-parameter subgroups.

2What is the form of every continuous one-parameter subgroup of a matrix Lie group?

It must turn addition of parameters into multiplication.

Exponentiation gives e^(sX)e^(tX)=e^((s+t)X), and every such subgroup arises this way.

3Which generator type produces a periodic, closed flow?

Expand the exponential and look for sine and cosine.

For X²=−I the series reduces to cos t·I + sin t·X, which closes after 2π.

4For the flow diag(eᵗ,e⁻ᵗ), what stays constant?

Multiply the two diagonal entries.

The determinant is eᵗ·e⁻ᵗ=1, which is why the flow lies in SL(2,R).

5If X²=0, what is eᵗˣ?

Every term from X² onward vanishes.

The exponential series terminates after two terms and gives a parabolic shear.
